faq.q: Which meeting apps does it work with?
faq.a: It listens to your computer's sound and your microphone, so it works next to any meeting app: Teams, Meet, Zoom, Skype, Webex and others. It does not connect to them or join your meeting.

faq.q: Do I have to press anything when a student asks a question?
faq.a: No. In auto mode it decides when a question has ended after a short pause. If you prefer, switch to manual mode and press the Question finished button yourself.
It depends on your AI service and connection. With a fast service such as Groq the first words can appear in about a second; free Gemini is slower, especially at busy times.
Yes. It remembers the last few questions and answers of the class, so 'and how do I do that in code?' is understood.

faq.q: Will my students see the assistant window?
faq.a: The window is excluded from screen capture by Windows, it draws its own mouse pointer inside the window, and it uses no tooltips or pop-up boxes. Different meeting apps behave differently, so always run a two-minute test call first.
No. Speech is turned into text on your own computer. Only the text of a detected question, your subject line and a few recent lines are sent to the AI service you chose.

faq.q: Is this for cheating in exams or interviews?
faq.a: No. ClassCue is built for teachers and trainers who want a private helper during their own lessons. Using it to cheat or to mislead others is against the Terms of use.

faq.q: Do I need my own AI key?
faq.a: Today, yes: a Google Gemini key (has a free tier), a Groq key (free plan, very fast) or an Anthropic Claude key. A plan with AI included is planned.

posts.title: How to handle tough student questions live (without freezing)
posts.summary: Five habits that keep you calm when a question comes out of nowhere.
body: Every teacher has had the moment: a student asks something you did not plan for, the room goes quiet, and you feel every second.

Repeat the question in your own words. It confirms you understood, it gives the class a moment to think, and it gives you time. 'So you are asking why the graph opens downwards when a is negative?' is a good start.
Give the one-sentence answer, then explain. People forgive a slow explanation, but not a long wait before any answer.
A real-life comparison does more than three definitions. Prepare one example for each big idea in the lesson.

body.h: 4. Say when you are not sure

body: 'I think it is this, let me check and confirm after the break' builds more trust than a confident guess that turns out wrong.
A private assistant that shows an answer line by line can help you stay fluent. Use it as a prompt, not a script: check facts you are unsure about before you state them as true.

posts.title: Staying private while sharing your screen: a two-minute test
posts.summary: A simple checklist to run before your first class with any private window.
body: Different meeting apps capture your screen in different ways. Never assume: test.
Start a meeting with a colleague, or join from a second account. Share your screen or the window you will teach from.

Ask them to confirm five things: they see your teaching content; they do not see the private window; they do not see a mouse pointer moving over empty space; no small hover text or pop-up box appears; and nothing flashes when you open settings.

Share a single window instead of the whole screen, change the way the meeting app captures, and run the test again. Choose your settings before you start sharing, because some drop-down lists are drawn by Windows.
Meeting apps update often. A two-minute test before each new term is cheap insurance.

posts.title: Free vs paid AI keys for teaching: what actually changes?
posts.summary: Speed, limits and privacy: how to pick an AI service for live classes.
body: Most private assistants send the text of a question to an AI service. You can use a free plan or a paid one. Here is what changes.
Fast services such as Groq return the first words in about a second. Free tiers of larger models can be slower, especially when many people use them.
Free plans limit how many requests you can make per minute and per day. In a lively class with many questions you may hit them.
On some free plans, the text you send may be used to improve the provider's products. Paid plans usually do not. Read the provider's current terms before sending anything about students.
Start with a free plan to learn the tool. If you use it every week, a paid key usually costs very little for light classroom use and removes the limits.
